analysis.one_liner: Expands the 60-day advance-notice requirement for plant closings and mass layoffs to far more workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate vote despite reaching the Senate calendar with 9 Democratic sponsors; it died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 1988 WARN law already requires most large employers to give workers 60 days notice before a plant closing or mass layoff. This bill would have covered far more businesses — those with 50 or more employees instead of 100 — and far more layoffs — those affecting 25 or more workers instead of 500 or more. It would also have paid affected workers double: their lost wages plus interest, plus an equal amount in liquidated damages, unless the employer showed good faith. Workers could have filed complaints with the Labor Department, which could investigate and sue on their behalf, instead of having to pay for a lawyer themselves.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies with 50 to 99 employees, and at any layoffs of 25 or more workers that fall under today's thresholds, would get advance notice — time to find a new job, arrange training, or plan for lost income. Workers who did get short notice would be owed their back pay plus interest, plus an equal amount in liquidated damages. Part-time workers would count toward coverage, and multi-site closings affecting 100 or more workers would be covered even if no single site crossed the old threshold.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing plant closings or large layoffs

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the employer-size threshold from 100 to 50 employees and the layoff threshold from 500 employees (or 50 if one-third of the site) to 25, and sets notice periods of 30, 60, or 90 days based on how many workers are affected [S2].

Doubles the penalty for short notice: employers owe back pay with interest plus an additional liquidated-damages amount equal to that sum, with the good-faith exemption limited to the damages and penalty rather than wiping out liability [S2].

Lets workers file a complaint with the Secretary of Labor or sue; the Labor Department must investigate and resolve complaints, gets subpoena power under the Fair Labor Standards Act, and can sue on workers' behalf to recover back pay, interest, benefits, and damages paid directly to employees [S2].

Extends coverage to part-time employees, requires notice to each affected worker personally (not just the union), counts related layoffs within a 30-day window toward the thresholds, and requires employers to post information about rights and how to file a complaint, with fines up to $100 per willful posting violation [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 50 or more employees — especially manufacturers, retailers, and multi-site companies planning restructurings — would face notice obligations for smaller layoffs, a longer maximum notice window of 90 days, and potentially doubled damages when they fail to give notice. The Labor Department would take on the cost of investigating complaints and enforcing the law.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would rise for mid-sized employers, since layoffs of 25 to 49 workers that are currently exempt would trigger notice and possible liability [S2].

Doubling damages and adding Department enforcement could increase litigation and settlement exposure for employers that miscalculate the new, more complicated tiered thresholds (30/60/90 days by layoff size, plus 30-day aggregation rules) [S2].

Advance-notice requirements can slow restructurings and may lead some employers to stage layoffs in smaller increments to stay under the thresholds, though the bill's aggregation rule targets exactly that practice [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For affected workers the benefit is concrete: weeks of warning and doubled recovery when notice is skipped. The cost falls on employers in the form of notice compliance and doubled damages, and on the Labor Department as new enforcement work. These are real but limited costs, and the good-faith exemption lets courts reduce penalties for honest mistakes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 1994, placed on the Senate calendar of business in April 1994, and then sat there until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995 without the Senate ever voting on it.

narrative.text: Senator Metzenbaum introduced the bill on March 24, 1994, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors: Kennedy, Simon, Mikulski, Pell, Wellstone, Riegle, and Feingold [S1,S4].
On April 11, 1994, the Senate read the bill a second time and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 407 [S1,S5].
No further action was taken — no committee report, no floor debate, no vote — and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1,S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with 50 or more employees kept the existing narrower WARN rules: no notice requirement for smaller layoffs, and back-pay liability without the doubled damages and department enforcement the bill would have added. Dislocated workers got nothing.

against.what_they_did: Placed the bill on the calendar in April 1994 but never brought it to the floor or to a committee markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats; the bill never reached a floor vote where the partisan split would have been recorded [S4].

industries.industry: Employers with 50+ employees (manufacturing, retail, and multi-site companies)
industries.note: These employers would face notice duties for far smaller layoffs, notice periods up to 90 days, and doubled damages for violations. Their compliance costs come out of the same restructurings that would otherwise proceed without warning to workers.
The bill gives the Department complaint intake, investigation, subpoena power under the FLSA, and authority to sue on workers' behalf, with recoveries paid directly to affected employees.
